issues.legal_issue: Demand and voluntary acceptance of illegal gratification, supported by reliable evidence, are sufficient to sustain a public-servant corruption conviction, with the statutory presumption applying once the foundational facts are established.
material_facts: The accused was a public servant who asked the complainant for money in connection with supplying an official land record.
At a trap, the complainant handed the accused the recorded, treated currency; the accused put it in a desk drawer and supplied the record.
The currency was recovered, and the complainant’s account was corroborated by a witness who accompanied him and by an official witness.
The record-delivery register bore the complainant’s signature and the date of the trap; the defence did not produce the register to support its claim that delivery had occurred earlier.
The court found no material discrepancy undermining the demand, acceptance, or recovery, and rejected the defence explanations.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution proved demand and voluntary acceptance beyond reasonable doubt; the conviction under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act was rightly sustained, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, demand of illegal gratification and its voluntary acceptance are essential to the offence; mere recovery is insufficient. Under Section 20, once the prosecution proves acceptance or obtaining of gratification as a foundational fact, the court presumes that it was accepted as a motive or reward, unless the accused proves otherwise. The prosecution must establish the foundational facts, while the accused may rebut the presumption on a preponderance of probabilities. The court applied State of Punjab v. Madan Mohan Lal Verma (2013) 14 SCC 153 and C.M. Sharma v. State of A.P. (2010) 15 SCC 1, and referred to Ram Prakash Arora v. State of Punjab, T. Subramanian v. State of T.N., State of Kerala v. C.P. Rao, and Mukut Bihari v. State of Rajasthan.

rule.if: corruption_conviction_appeal and official_gratification_demand_proved and voluntary_acceptance_proved and recovery_corrobated_by_evidence and defence_explanation_unpersuasive

predicates.corruption_conviction_appeal: The matter is an appeal challenging a conviction for a public-servant corruption offence.
predicates.official_gratification_demand_proved: The prosecution proves that the public servant demanded gratification in connection with an official act.
predicates.voluntary_acceptance_proved: The prosecution proves that the public servant voluntarily accepted the gratification as a bribe.
predicates.recovery_corrobated_by_evidence: The recovery of the gratification is supported by reliable evidence corroborating the account of the demand and acceptance.
predicates.defence_explanation_unpersuasive: The accused does not provide a persuasive explanation sufficient to rebut the inference arising from the proved foundational facts.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a corruption conviction and the demand, voluntary acceptance, and corroborating recovery evidence are proved while the defence explanation is unpersuasive, the conviction is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to send a phenolphthalein handwash sample for chemical examination does not, by itself, invalidate trap evidence where recovery and the accused’s handling of the gratification are established by direct evidence.
material_facts: A trap was conducted using currency treated with phenolphthalein powder.
The accused accepted the currency and put it in a desk drawer, from which the currency was recovered and identified.
The accused’s handwash solution turned pink, but the collected solution was not sent for chemical examination.
The court found no evidence that investigators shook hands with or caught the accused’s hands, and relied on direct evidence of the recovery.
issues.conclusion: The absence of chemical examination of the handwash sample did not undermine the prosecution case or make the conviction unsafe.
issues.legal_principle: The phenolphthalein test and chemical examination of its solution are not statutory requirements for proving a trap. The test is used for the satisfaction of officials, and its absence is not fatal where direct evidence proves recovery and the relevant conduct. The court applied State of U.P. v. Zakaullah (1998) 1 SCC 557.

rule.if: corruption_trap_case and handwash_sample_not_chemically_examined and direct_evidence_proves_gratification_recovery and no_evidence_of_transfer_from_investigator

predicates.corruption_trap_case: The proceeding concerns a trap conducted to prove a public-servant corruption offence.
predicates.handwash_sample_not_chemically_examined: The handwash solution collected during the trap is not sent for chemical examination.
predicates.direct_evidence_proves_gratification_rec: Witnesses or other direct evidence establish the recovery of the treated gratification from the accused’s custody.
predicates.no_evidence_of_transfer_from_investigato: There is no evidence that contact with an investigator transferred the test substance to the accused.

issues.definition: When a trap case has an unexamined handwash sample but direct evidence proves recovery and no investigator-to-accused transfer is shown, the failure to examine the sample does not invalidate the trap evidence.
